doc.title: Bill Easley interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 1, 2021

title: Sophisticated Ladies and choosing stability
summary: Joining the Ellington band under Mercer, moving back to New York for Sophisticated Ladies, turning down Blakey and Silver.

bands.name: Panama Francis and the Savoy Sultans
Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: So I want to ask you about the Broadway pit band part of your career.
Those are fairly coveted gigs, aren’t they?

Yup. Absolutely. And “Sophisticated Ladies” was the Broadway show. And that came about because of the fact that I had been out — I had been out on the road — right after Duke died I went out with the band for about [gap] months or whatever. But the reason I went out with the band was because Stanley Dance had told Mercer, “Man, you’ve got to find a clarinet player, because the clarinet is a very important voice in Ellingtonia.” And actually it was Jimmy Hamilton had recommended or suggested that I get the gig after he left the band. But it never did materialize at that time. But right after Duke died I went out on the band with Mercer and the only reason I went out was because I was working with Isaac Hayes at that time and this was during a period where he was out making a movie somewhere or something like that. Regarding the band, Mercer was, he said, “Man, you’ve got an open chair in the band any time you want to come back.” So when he came through Memphis one time and they were getting ready, talking about doing a musical on Broadway. So Mercer invited me to come, you know, if you want to come back. So I moved back to New York with the promise of this job on Broadway. And it’s sort of what I aspired, the type of work that I aspired to do in my lifetime. I turned down two months when I got to New York in January of 1980, there were three possibilities: going out with Horace Silver, Art Blakey, and going out with Panama Francis and the Savoy Sultans you see. To make a long story short I went out on the road, I turned down the gigs with Blakey and Horace Silver. Because first of all jazz sidemen are the most underpaid workers probably since, you know I don’t even want to say. But that’s just the history of jazz sidemen, there was some money but jazz sidemen in America are some of the most mistreated people on the planet. And you probably know about that so I won’t — I’ll spare you the details of how the jazz thing works. So I had a half a jazz career but I’ve been at enough Broadway shows and enough recording that was more geared toward stability than creativity. I know I talk a lot man. Jump in anytime, because —
Those are great — stability and creativity — I think that’s very important for musicians to have a balance there because if they only have stability they’ll be one of those grumpy people who just —
Yeah there’s a lot of those, right?
